title: Night- to-Night Variability in Sleep Disordered Breathing: Sex-Related Predictors and Impact on Obstructive Sleep Apnea Clinical Heterogeneity
text: Expected outcomes. We will identify sleep and respiratory traits with biologically plausible effects on daytime function and determine the role of sex on these associations. Results of this study have the potential to promote a significant paradigm change on how we define OSA severity for both women and men and will contribute to reducing sex disparities in OSA

title: Exploiting emerging ideas in G protein-coupled receptor biology and pharmacology to treat asthma
text:
Overview Project Narrative
Asthma is a complex syndrome with significant health and economic impacts, affecting over 25 million people
in the US. This multi-project proposal seeks to establish new ways to target mechanisms that cause asthma,
by focusing on the development of new drugs and new strategies that can be rapidly translated to the clinic.

title: Identifying and targeting collateral lethal vulnerabilities in cancers
text:
When cancer cells sustain deletion of a tumor suppressor gene, neighboring genes are invariably co-deleted.
When the passenger deleted gene is a member of a gene family that encodes a cell essential function, the
redundant gene (co-expressed paralog) residing elsewhere in the genome represents a cancer-specific
vulnerability that would spare normal cells with intact genomes. We believe that this proposed research study
will identify multiple novel drug targets for cancer treatment, thereby improving outcomes and prolonging
patients’ lives.

title: Bridging Gaps to Translate Plasma Alzheimer's Disease Biomarkers to Diverse Populations
text:
As the global burden of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) is expected to triple over the
next thirty years, there is an urgent public health need for scalable and cost-effective diagnostic tools that can
be applied across diverse, international populations. The proposed project is highly relevant to public health
by advancing promising ADRD plasma biomarkers towards appropriate clinical and research use in
populations that stand to benefit the most by supporting diagnosis, personalized interventions and public health
strategies. This project closely aligns with NIA research priorities to understand AD in diverse populations, the
impact of biology and personal factors on age-related disease prognosis, and special interest in fostering
ADRD research in Africa.

title: Contribution of myeloid cells to the anti-tumor adaptive immune response after radiation in a pediatric brain tumor
text:
Brain tumor is the leading cause of death by cancer in the pediatric population; thus there is a great need for
novel therapies. Radiation is an important part of therapy for many high-grade tumors including medulloblastoma,
the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, but it is rarely curative and comes with significant side effects.
This project aims to identify reversible causes of immune suppression in medulloblastomas treated with radiation
so that we can leverage the benefits of immunotherapy to achieve long-term remission for patients with
treatment-resistant tumors.

title: Using Novel Machine Learning Approaches to Understand Subgingival Microbiome Heterogeneity in Relation to Health and Disease
text:
The proposed research will use an integrative approach coupling population-based oral microbiome data with
novel machine learning techniques to understand species and strain level microbiome heterogeneity and its
relationship to periodontitis clinical phenotypes also accounting for various environmental and medical exposures.
The findings of this study will significantly advance our understanding of the subgingival microbiome elucidating
different microbiome states and their associations with periodontitis offering opportunities for developing targeted,
personalized treatment strategies. This study aligns closely with the special interest of NIDCR (NOT-DE-23-002)
that calls for projects utilizing data science resources and methods for dental, oral, and craniofacial research.

title: A phase I study of RNA-lipid particle vaccines for newly-diagnosed glioblastoma, IND19304 08/21/2020
text:
Despite maximal surgery, radiation and chemotherapy, glioblastoma (GBM) remains invariably recalcitrant, and
necessitates development of new therapies. We have developed a novel FDA-IND approved agent (BB-19304,
Sayour) utilizing RNA-lipid nanoparticles (RNA-LPs) to reprogram innate/adaptive immunity against GBM. In this
proposal, we will explore the safety, maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and immunologic activity of RNA-LPs in a
first-in-human clinical trial (NCT04573140) for patients with newly-diagnosed GBM.

title: Midwest AViDD Center
text:
Overall – Midwest AViDD Center
NARRATIVE
 The Midwest AViDD Center is comprised of a highly experienced, integrated, and multidisciplinary team with
the common goal of developing inhibitors of SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses of pandemic concern. We utilize a
balance of innovative and proven approaches and technologies to develop inhibitors to established druggable
processes (viral entry and proteolytic cleavage) as well as less conventional but equally essential viral processes
(nuclease and helicase activities). We aim to deliver novel inhibitors that can be developed into effective orally
available drugs that potently and safely suppress virus replication and help prevent infections as well as adverse
clinical outcomes including death.

title: Early TMS-EEG potentials as biomarkers for personalized neuromodulation in treatment-resistant depression
text:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is an FDA-cleared treatment for depression, but only about
half of patients show sustained improvement, partly due to our inability to tailor treatment parameters to individual
brain responses. This research uses an EEG brain biomarker of prefrontal activity to guide personalized rTMS
treatment. This personalized approach could significantly improve the efficacy and efficiency of rTMS treatment
and advance our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying successful depression treatment.

title: Targets, Structures and Drugs
text: Targets, Structures and Drugs (TSD) Research Program Project Summary The mission of the Targets, Structures, and Drugs (TSD) Program is to accelerate the development of novel therapies for cancer treatment by identifying lead compounds or macromolecular target structures, progressing their development via medicinal chemistry lead optimization and rational design, and testing in preclinical evaluation using animal models, including naturally occurring canine models that are highly reflective of human disease. In the 2020-25 cycle, TSD members have shepherded eight therapies into FDA-approved drugs or human clinical trials and 75 compounds into the development pipeline from 2020-2025. TSD members have also led 40 canine studies, including 19 therapy trials in companion dogs with cancer to evaluate PICR leads of new and strategically repurposed drugs, as well as novel technologies. TSD comprises three clusters: Target Validation (led by Deborah Knapp), Chemical and Structure Biology (led by John Tesmer), and Medicinal Chemistry (led by Emily Dykhuizen). Members of the TSD Program have leadership stakes in nationally recognized cancer programs such as the NCI Integrated Canine Data Commons, the NCI Comparative Oncology Clinical Trials Consortium, and DARPA Make It, as well as in the governance of the Purdue Institute for Drug Discovery and the Purdue Institute of Inflammation, Immunology and Infectious Disease. TSD co-leaders also serve as directors for two NIH T32 training programs in Molecular Biophysics and Drug Discovery. Over the last cycle, TSD scientists secured just under $12 million in peer- reviewed cancer-related support (up from $9.7 million last renewal) and have published 562 cancer-related peer- reviewed articles (up from 505 last renewal). Of these papers, 23% were high-impact, and 12% involved intra- programmatic collaborations, 17% inter-programmatic, and 49% inter-institutional (similar to last renewal). Furthermore, TSD faculty successfully translated their research into key deliverables, including 69 patents (up from 53 in last renewal), of which 25 were licensed, and 8 startup companies in the cancer space. In this cycle, TSD plans to: (1) enhance small molecule drug discovery and development of biological therapeutics; (2) accelerate movement of discoveries toward clinical application; and (3) catalyze collaborative interactions to increase targeted therapeutic development. In parallel with these goals, TSD will continue to recruit scientists in the areas of drug discovery, chemical biology, and cryo-electron microscopy/tomography, contribute to rigorous training for junior investigators through TSD Program activities and cancer-relevant T32 predoctoral fellowship programs, and mentor junior faculty to become world-class cancer researchers.

title: Investigating the mechanisms that make jumbophages impervious to bacterial immune systems
text:
Bacterial viruses, called phages, infect and kill bacteria and thus represent a potential alternative to antibiotics.
However, bacteria are equipped with diverse immune systems that prevent phage replication. We have identified
a phage family possessing the most potent immune evasion tactics discovered to date, and will characterize
their molecular mechanisms to identify and develop better phage therapeutics.

title: Determining the functional epigenomic consequences of HPV viral oncogene expression heterogeneity in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
text:
HPV+ oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) poses a substantial and rising burden, without clear
biomarkers for risk stratification or treatment options for patients with poor treatment response. Suppression of
HPV viral gene expression in HPV+ tumors has emerged as a potential mechanism by which tumor cells adopt
a distinct cell state (termed HPVoff) with phenotypes contributing to worse clinical outcomes. In this proposal, we
aim to identify key regulators and downstream mediators of the HPVoff state that may serve as novel therapeutic
targets or biomarkers to inform clinical management of patients with HPV+ OPSCC.

title: Genome-Wide fitness analysis of Group B Streptococcus in intestinal colonization
text:
Late-onset (LO) Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus [GBS]) infection (occurring at >7 days of
life) is the most common manifestation of invasive GBS disease in infants, and gastrointestinal (GI)
colonization is an established precursor. To identify and validate GBS factors that promote GI colonization, we
will apply Tn-seq, a transposon insertion sequencing methodology, in an established murine model of GBS
colonization. We will determine GBS genes essential for colonization with the purpose of identifying target
genes for novel diagnostic and therapeutic interventions.

title: Bioinformatics and Biostatistics
text: Cardiovascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, are a major cause of death globally. Lipid-lowering therapies and interventions lower the risk of major adverse clinical events such as myocardial infarction, but significant residual risk remains. The proposed Program, “Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms of Atherosclerosis,” seeks to better understand this residual risk and investigate possible mechanisms and interventions that could further lower cardiovascular risk. The Program focuses on mechanisms of atherosclerotic plaque stabilization and destabilization, with a focus on macrophages and their functions. Core B, Bioinformatics and Biostatistics, will provide state of the art, coordinated services to the Program as a whole, and thus help the Program achieve its overall goals. These services include (A) bioinformatic analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data; B) bioinformatic analysis of CITE-seq data; C) bioinformatic analysis of bulk RNA-seq data; and D) biostatistical support for study design, power, and correlative analyses. All Projects will use Core B services equally. The use of Core B will enable application of state of the art bioinformatic and biostatistical analyses in consistent, integrated and coordinated analysis pipelines within and across all three Projects for maximum scientific inference, translation and impact as well as highest standards of reproducibility and comparison among all Projects of the PPG Program and for data resource sharing and dissemination.

title: Evaluating Comparative Effectiveness of Glucose-lowering Therapy in People with HIV and Type 2 Diabetes
text:
This project will study how different glucose-lowering medications work in people with HIV and diabetes, who
face unique metabolic challenges related to both HIV infection and its treatment. Within a large, multi-site
cohort of people with HIV and diabetes, we will compare the effectiveness of five common classes of glucose-
lowering medications on glycemic control, as well as cardiovascular and kidney outcomes. The findings will
help guide better treatment decisions for this growing and understudied population.

title: microGRID-MALDI2-timsTOF fleX mass spectrometry imaging system
text: The microGRID-MALDI2-timsTOF flex imaging mass spectrometer will provide UC San Diego researchers with single-cell, high-resolution spatial metabolomics capabilities that are currently unavailable on campus or in the region. Coupled with the METASPACE metabolite-annotation software platform and the PI’s proven track record in developing and democratizing spatial and single-cell technologies, lowering barriers through user-friendly software, and leading two prior core facilities, this instrument will accelerate NIH-funded research in cancer metabolism, microbiome host interactions, and drug discovery ultimately advancing the understanding and treatment of human disease.

title: Single Cell Analysis Core
text: A central goal of this P01 program project is the comprehensive interrogation of how cellular senescence affects the gene expression, phenotype, and function of diverse cell populations in various tissues following infection or vaccination. As traditional single-cell omics omits critical phenotypic and spatial information, the Single-Cell Analysis core will provide with innovative approaches to accurately identify immune cell populations and their functionality in their spatial context. This will be achieved by providing a consistent and validated pipeline of multiple high-throughput omics approaches including, single-cell RNA sequencing, cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing, cytometry by time of flight, spatial transcriptomics, and mass imaging. Interpretation of these data and their integration between the individual Projects will require a consistent experimental design and sample acquisition, as well as a significant effort of bioinformaticians with expertise in the biology of aging, immunology, and single-cell analysis. The Specific Aims of the Single-cell Analysis Core are: 1) Provide a quality-controlled platform and custom reagents for the single-cell and spatial genomics assessment of senescent cells; 2) Provide bioinformatics and statistical analyses of single-cell and spatial omics datasets; and 3) Develop a database to warehouse, integrate, and share datasets.

title: CYTOSCAPE: AN ECOSYSTEM FOR NETWORK GENOMICS
text:
CYTOSCAPE: AN ECOSYSTEM FOR NETWORK GENOMICS
NARRATIVE
Support of Cytoscape as a U24 Community Resource will enable NIH investigators to maintain and magnify
their ongoing successful efforts to apply molecular network knowledge to identify new pathways, biomarkers,
drug targets and genetic variants underlying disease.

title: Integrated mass spectrometry-based chemoproteomic and genomic technologies for studying dynamic kinase interactomes
text:
PROGRAM NARRATIVE
Protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction (PPI and PDI) networks control virtually all cellular processes, and
they are commonly perturbed by devastating human diseases. To overcome key challenges in interaction
network analysis, we will develop novel, transformative bioanalytical methods to quantify cellular PPI and PDI
networks and their dynamic perturbation in disease, thereby enabling groundbreaking, broadly relevant
discoveries of disease mechanisms and drug targets. We will apply our methods to unravel the interaction
networks that control cellular plasticity, a biological process driving diverse pathological processes, including
cancer metastasis, organ fibrosis, viral infection, drug resistance, and immune escape.

title: Mechanisms of Endosomal Signaling of Itch
text:
Itch is a common sensory experience that allows for the detection of noxious substances and incites their
removal by scratching that can be debilitating if not properly controlled. Advances in our understanding of the
itch-specific neural pathway have highlighted many G protein-coupled receptors needed to transmit itch, and
new discoveries in sensory neurons have emphasized the importance of G protein-coupled receptor signaling
from subcellular domains to convey sensory stimuli. This research project seeks to link these new discoveries,
to determine the importance of endosomal signaling of GPCRs in itch and to characterize new targets for
improved therapeutics to treat pruritus.
